Why Driver and Carrier Verification Is Becoming a Bigger Business Priority in 2026
September 12, 2026
4 min read
DRIVER VERIFICATION
CARRIER VERIFICATION
COMPLIANCE
RISK MANAGEMENT
SENTINEL

Driver and carrier verification has always been part of the trucking business, but lately it is no longer just an administrative step buried inside the hiring or onboarding process. It has become a bigger business priority tied directly to safety, compliance, insurance, liability and operational trust. For motor carriers, brokers and fleet operators, knowing who they are working with, what their history looks like and whether documentation is complete can make a major difference in how protected the business is over time.

Verification Is No Longer Just Paperwork

For years, many transportation companies have relied on self-reported driver histories, manual reference checks, phone calls, paperwork and scattered data sources to make hiring decisions. That might include chasing previous employers, waiting on delayed responses, re-entering information into different systems and trying to make sense of incomplete records. The problem is that trucking moves too fast for slow or scattered verification. A missing job, unexplained employment gap or undisclosed safety issue can create risk that may not show up until later, when it becomes much more expensive to fix.

In trucking, who you put behind the wheel matters. A driver qualification file is not just paperwork. It is part of a carrier's proof that it followed a responsible process, checked the right information and made a hiring decision based on accurate records. When work history, MVRs, drug testing updates, employment verification and safety documentation are incomplete or spread across disconnected systems, it becomes harder for fleets to prove consistency and accountability. That can create compliance problems, insurance concerns, liability exposure and additional stress for safety and recruiting teams.

How Sentinel Helps Fleets Modernize Verification

This is where platforms like Sentinel by Spotter AI are helping fleets move verification out of the manual, reactive category and into a more organized system. Sentinel is designed to support hiring, recruiting and compliance workflows by helping motor carriers manage driver applications, secure document uploads, employment verification, MVR monitoring, drug testing updates, safety records, risk scoring and real-time submission tracking from one place. Instead of relying on several separate tools and hoping nothing gets missed, fleets can create a cleaner process with better visibility into each driver's status.

The operational benefits are just as important as the compliance benefits. Faster verification can help recruiters move qualified drivers through onboarding more efficiently, which matters in a market where good drivers may not stay available for long. Real-time alerts can help teams know when drug tests clear or when driver record changes appear, instead of waiting on manual follow-ups or delayed reports. Cleaner documentation can also reduce back-office confusion and give safety and compliance teams more confidence that important steps are being tracked properly.

Verification as a Risk Management Strategy

The old way of verification was built around phone tag, paperwork, delayed responses, duplicate data entry and onboarding limbo. The new way is built around structured data, faster verification, cleaner records, better visibility and smarter hiring decisions. When work history verification is connected with broader screening data such as MVRs, drug testing and compliance records, it becomes much more than a box to check. It becomes a smarter way to hire and a stronger way to protect the business.

In 2026 and beyond, verification should be treated as part of a carrier's risk management strategy, not just another hiring task. Fleets that invest in stronger verification systems will be better positioned to improve compliance, reduce risk, hire faster and keep their operations moving with greater confidence. Trucking will always depend on people, experience and judgment, but modern fleets need better tools to make sure those decisions are backed by reliable information. For carriers looking to operate with more protection and less uncertainty, cleaner verification is becoming a smart place to start.

MVR Screening for Small Fleets vs Large Carriers

5 min read
SMALL FLEETS
MVR

SENTINEL

Small fleets and large carriers have different screening needs. Large carriers need continuous monitoring, deep integrations and enterprise workflows across thousands of drivers. Small fleets need fast, affordable, pay-per-use checks without subscriptions or long contracts. Matching the tool to fleet size is the difference between overpaying for features you will never use and staying compliant on a budget. Sentinel lets a small fleet screen as fast as a large one with a Safety Score powered by AI.

Key takeaways
Large carriers optimize for scale, monitoring and integration.
Small fleets optimize for cost, speed and simplicity.
Subscriptions and quote-based contracts often overcharge small fleets.
Sentinel keeps small carriers compliant with pay-per-use pricing and a free first MVR.
How screening needs change with fleet size

The federal rules are the same for everyone: pull an MVR at hire and annually, run PSP and Clearinghouse checks, keep a complete DQ file. What changes is volume and resources. A carrier with thousands of drivers and a dedicated safety team screens differently from an owner-operator running a handful of trucks.

What large carriers need
Continuous monitoring across a large roster so new violations surface immediately.
Integrations with existing HR, recruiting and telematics systems.
Enterprise workflows and reporting for a dedicated safety department.
Volume pricing that fits constant, year-round hiring.
What small fleets need
Low, predictable cost with no monthly fee between hires.
Speed, so a good driver is not lost to a faster carrier.
Simplicity, because there is rarely a full-time safety team.
A clear risk read instead of raw records to interpret alone.
Where each type of tool fits
FLEET PROFILE	PRIMARY NEED	BEST TOOL TYPE
Owner-operator to small fleet	Cost control and speed	Pay-per-use, all-in-one screening
Growing mid-size fleet	Balance of cost and coverage	Pay-per-use or light monitoring
Large carrier	Scale, monitoring, integration	Enterprise monitoring platform
Why subscriptions hurt small fleets

A monthly or quote-based contract assumes steady, high-volume screening. A small fleet that hires a few drivers a quarter still pays every month, so the real cost per useful check climbs. Pay-per-use removes that waste by charging only when you actually pull a record.

Driver safety tools for small carriers

Sentinel is built for exactly this profile. It consolidates MVR, PSP, CDLIS and background into one check, returns a Safety Score powered by AI in under 60 seconds, charges pay-per-use with no monthly subscription, and gives you the first MVR free. A small carrier stays compliant and screens as fast as a large one, without carrying an enterprise contract.

Frequently asked questions
Do small fleets need the same screening as large carriers?

The federal requirements are the same. The difference is that small fleets benefit from pay-per-use pricing and simplicity, while large carriers need monitoring and integration at scale.

What is the best driver screening tool for a small carrier?

A fast, consolidated, pay-per-use tool with no subscription. Sentinel fits that need with a free first MVR and a Safety Score powered by AI.

Is continuous monitoring worth it for a small fleet?

It can add cost with limited added signal on a small, stable roster. Many small fleets do better matching monitoring to risk and using pay-per-use checks.

How to Read a CDL MVR Report

6 min read

SENTINEL

A CDL MVR report is the official driving history a state DMV keeps on a commercial driver. To read one, work through five things in order: license status and class, endorsements and restrictions, the violation history, crashes, and any suspensions or withdrawals. For a CDL-A driver, the report tells you whether the license is valid, whether the driver is legally qualified to operate a commercial motor vehicle, and whether the record shows patterns that raise safety or insurance risk. Sentinel reads it for you and returns a Safety Score powered by AI so you act on a clear risk read instead of raw DMV codes.

Key takeaways
An MVR shows license status, class, endorsements, restrictions, violations, crashes and suspensions.
For CDL drivers, focus on serious and major violations and repeat patterns, not just point totals.
FMCSA requires an MVR at hire and at least once every 12 months for every driver.
Sentinel consolidates the MVR and returns a Safety Score powered by AI in under 60 seconds.
What is a CDL MVR report?

MVR stands for Motor Vehicle Record. It is the driving history that each state motor vehicle agency keeps on a licensed driver. A CDL MVR is the same record for a commercial driver, and it carries extra weight because commercial vehicles cause more damage in a crash and are held to a higher federal standard. When you run an MVR check on a CDL-A driver, you are confirming the person is qualified and safe to put behind the wheel of a tractor trailer.

What information is on an MVR report?

Most CDL motor vehicle records include the same core sections, though the exact layout changes from state to state:

Driver and license details: name, date of birth, license number, license class (A, B or C) and issue and expiration dates.
License status: valid, suspended, revoked, cancelled or disqualified.
Endorsements: H (hazmat), N (tanker), T (doubles and triples), P (passenger), S (school bus) and X (hazmat and tanker combined).
Restrictions: for example air brake restrictions or corrective lens requirements.
Violation history: moving violations, convictions and their dates.
Crash and accident records where the state reports them.
Suspensions, revocations and out-of-service actions.
How to read a CDL MVR step by step
Check license status first. If the license is suspended, revoked or disqualified, nothing else matters. The driver cannot legally operate.
Confirm class and endorsements. A CDL-A driver hauling hazmat needs the H or X endorsement. Missing endorsements are a compliance gap you have to fix before dispatch.
Read the violation history. Look at what happened, when, and how often. One old minor violation is very different from three speeding convictions in eighteen months.
Flag serious and major violations. These carry federal disqualification consequences and are the strongest risk signals on the record.
Review crashes and out-of-service actions. A pattern of preventable crashes or out-of-service orders points to elevated risk.
Which CDL violations matter most?

Under federal rules, some violations are treated as serious and others as major. Serious violations include excessive speeding of 15 mph or more over the limit, reckless driving, improper or erratic lane changes, following too closely, and using a handheld phone or texting while driving a commercial vehicle. Major violations include driving under the influence, leaving the scene of an accident, and using a commercial vehicle to commit a felony. Repeated serious violations can disqualify a CDL driver, so they matter far more than a single low point count.

How violation codes work across states

Every state writes violations differently, which makes raw records hard to compare. The AAMVA Code Dictionary, known as ACD codes, standardizes convictions and withdrawals into a common set so the same offense reads the same way no matter which state issued it. Screening tools that normalize ACD codes let you compare drivers fairly instead of guessing what each state abbreviation means.

How often do you need to pull an MVR?

FMCSA requires an MVR at the time of hire and a review at least once every 12 months for each driver you employ. Many fleets go further and monitor records continuously so a new suspension or violation shows up right away rather than at the next annual review.

How Sentinel makes reading an MVR faster

It shows license status and class, endorsements and restrictions, moving violations and convictions, crashes where reported, and any suspensions or disqualifications on the commercial license.

How far back does a CDL MVR go?

Most states report three to seven years of driving history, though serious commercial violations and disqualifications can appear for longer depending on the state.

Is an MVR the same as a PSP report?

No. An MVR comes from the state DMV and covers license and violation history. A PSP report comes from FMCSA and covers roadside inspections and crashes. Complete screening uses both, and Sentinel pulls them together.

What Is FMCSA Driver Safety Compliance
August 30, 2026
6 min read
FMCSA
COMPLIANCE
DRIVER QUALIFICATION FILE
MVR
SENTINEL

FMCSA driver safety compliance means meeting the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration rules for qualifying, screening and monitoring commercial drivers so your fleet stays legal and safe. In practice it covers the Driver Qualification File, motor vehicle record checks at hire and annually, Pre-Employment Screening Program reports, Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse queries, medical certification and hours-of-service rules. Staying compliant protects your operating authority, keeps your CSA scores clean and lowers your insurance and negligent hiring risk. Sentinel runs the screening pieces from one place so the file stays complete.

Key takeaways
Compliance centers on the Driver Qualification File required under 49 CFR 391.51.
MVR checks are required at hire and at least every 12 months.
PSP reports and Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse queries are part of a complete screen.
Non-compliance risks fines, out-of-service orders, higher insurance and negligent hiring lawsuits.
What does FMCSA compliance cover?

FMCSA sets the federal safety rules for interstate motor carriers. Driver safety compliance is the part of those rules that deals with who you let drive and how you keep proving they are qualified. It runs from the moment an applicant fills out a form through every year they stay on your roster.

The Driver Qualification File

The Driver Qualification File, or DQ file, is the core compliance record for each driver, required under 49 CFR 391.51. A complete file generally includes:

The employment application.
The motor vehicle record obtained at hire and the annual MVR review.
A copy of the CDL and verification of license status.
The road test certificate or equivalent.
The DOT medical examiner certificate.
Safety performance history from previous employers covering the prior three years.
The annual list of violations signed by the driver.
MVR checks at hire and annually

You must pull an MVR when you hire a driver and review one at least once every 12 months. The annual review confirms the driver still meets your standards and has not picked up disqualifying violations since the last check.

PSP reports

The Pre-Employment Screening Program is an FMCSA service that pulls a driver’s roadside inspection and crash history from the Motor Carrier Management Information System. A PSP report typically shows five years of crash data and three years of inspection history, which reveals patterns a state MVR alone will miss.

Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse

Before a CDL driver performs safety-sensitive functions, you must run a full pre-employment query in the FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse, and you must run a limited query at least once a year for current drivers. The Clearinghouse flags positive tests, refusals and incomplete return-to-duty processes.

License verification and medical certification

CDLIS, the Commercial Driver License Information System, confirms the license is valid and that the driver does not hold licenses in multiple states. The DOT physical and medical examiner certificate confirm the driver is medically fit to operate.

CSA scores and the Safety Measurement System

Compliance Safety Accountability, or CSA, is how FMCSA tracks carrier safety. The Safety Measurement System groups violations into categories called BASICs, including unsafe driving and driver fitness. Poor screening feeds bad scores, and bad scores raise insurance costs and audit risk.

What happens if you are not compliant?

Gaps in driver qualification and screening expose you to civil penalties, out-of-service orders during audits, higher insurance premiums, and negligent hiring liability if a poorly screened driver is involved in a crash. Compliance is cheaper than any one of those outcomes.

Instead of stitching together separate vendors for MVR, PSP, CDLIS and background checks, Sentinel runs them from one place and returns a single Safety Score powered by AI, so safety managers can keep DQ files complete and current without juggling logins or subscriptions.

What is the difference between MVR and PSP in FMCSA compliance?

The MVR is a state DMV record of license status and violations. The PSP is an FMCSA report of roadside inspections and crashes. A compliant screen uses both.

How often are MVR reviews required?

At hire and at least once every 12 months for each driver, under 49 CFR 391.25.

Is the Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse mandatory?

Yes. A full pre-employment query is required before a driver performs safety-sensitive work, and a limited query is required at least annually.

From Risk to Reliability: Rethinking Driver Work History Verification in 2026
June 30, 2026
6 min read
DRIVER VERIFICATION
WORK HISTORY
SENTINEL
COMPLIANCE
FLEET SAFETY
TRUCKING TECHNOLOGY
DRIVER RECRUITING

Automated work history verification is quickly becoming a critical part of modern trucking operations, and for good reason. For years, fleets have relied on self-reported driver histories, manual reference checks, phone calls, paperwork, and scattered data sources to make hiring decisions. The process has always been slow, but today the risk is much bigger than inconvenience.

In trucking, who you put behind the wheel matters.

A missing job, an unexplained gap, or an undisclosed safety issue is not just an HR headache. It can become a compliance problem, an insurance concern, a safety risk, a liability issue, and added stress for recruiting and safety teams already working under pressure. When fleets are expected to keep driver qualification files accurate and up to date, incomplete work history is more than a paperwork problem. It is a risk that can show up later in the worst possible way.

The Real Cost of Manual Verification

Manual verification also creates very real operational headaches. Recruiters spend valuable time chasing previous employers, waiting on delayed responses, re-entering the same information into different systems, and trying to make sense of incomplete records. Meanwhile, a qualified driver may be stuck in onboarding limbo, a truck may sit idle, and the fleet loses time and money it cannot afford to waste.

Manual verification can quietly become one of the most expensive bottlenecks in the hiring process.

In an industry where every minute and mile counts, delays in hiring are not just frustrating - they can directly impact revenue, equipment utilization, driver satisfaction, and the ability to keep freight moving. A slow verification process can also give another carrier the chance to hire a qualified driver first.

What Incomplete Work History Actually Puts at Risk

The risk of incomplete work history extends further than most fleets realize. Common exposures include:

Missing jobs and unexplained employment gaps
Undisclosed safety incidents or violations
Compliance problems with driver qualification file requirements
Insurance scrutiny and potential premium increases
Liability exposure following an incident involving an unvetted driver
Delayed onboarding that costs the fleet time and competitive position
Why the Stakes Are Higher in 2026

Today's environment demands a higher standard of accuracy and speed. Regulatory pressure remains high, insurance scrutiny is not easing up, and fleets are under more pressure to prove they are hiring responsibly. FMCSA requirements around driver qualification files and previous employer safety performance history already make verification a serious compliance issue. Industry research continues to point to insurance costs and lawsuit exposure as major concerns for motor carriers.

The trucking industry has always been the backbone of the economy, but its recruiting model is increasingly stuck in the past. While freight demand evolves, technology accelerates, and regulatory pressure intensifies, many fleets are still relying on outdated hiring processes built for a different era.

Today, the gap between how fleets recruit drivers and how the industry actually operates has never been wider. And that gap is costing companies time, money, safety, and competitive advantage.

Recent innovations from companies like Spotter AI highlight just how quickly the industry is shifting. With platforms like Sentinel from Spotter AI, fleets are beginning to move away from manual processes toward fully automated, intelligence-driven hiring systems.

The Problem with Traditional Recruiting

Traditional driver recruiting is largely manual, fragmented, and reactive. Recruiters spend hours gathering data from multiple sources, verifying work history, checking compliance records, and making judgment calls based on incomplete information.

This approach creates several critical issues:

Slow hiring timelines that cause fleets to lose qualified drivers to faster competitors
Inconsistent screening standards across recruiters and locations
Limited visibility into real risk factors
High administrative costs due to redundant processes and multiple vendors

In a market where speed and accuracy are everything, these inefficiencies are no longer sustainable.

The Rise of AI in Driver Hiring

Artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing how fleets approach recruiting. Instead of manually piecing together driver profiles, AI platforms can aggregate, analyze, and verify data in real time.

Solutions like Sentinel from Spotter AI are designed to consolidate multiple screening steps into a single workflow, pulling together critical data such as MVRs, PSP reports, and FMCSA records automatically.

This shift enables:

Instant qualification decisions
Automated retrieval and verification of driver records
Standardized screening criteria across the organization
Continuous monitoring instead of one-time checks

The result is a hiring process that moves from days to seconds - without sacrificing accuracy or compliance.

Safety Is Now a Data Problem

Hiring the wrong driver is not just a recruiting issue - it is a safety and financial liability.

Traditional models rely on static background checks, which provide only a snapshot in time. But risk is dynamic. Driver behavior, violations, and compliance status can change rapidly.

Modern platforms, including Sentinel from Spotter AI, use predictive analytics to assess risk continuously. By analyzing patterns across multiple data sources, fleets can identify high-risk drivers before incidents occur.

This proactive approach shifts safety from reactive damage control to preventative strategy.

Compliance Has Become Real Time

Regulatory requirements are becoming more complex, and enforcement is becoming more data-driven. Maintaining compliant driver qualification files manually is both time-consuming and error-prone.

Automation changes the equation entirely.

With AI-driven systems like those developed by Spotter AI, compliance is no longer a periodic task. It becomes a continuous, real-time process where data is automatically updated, verified, and flagged when issues arise.

This reduces the risk of violations, simplifies audits, and ensures fleets are always inspection-ready.

The Hidden Cost of Inefficiency

Many fleets underestimate the true cost of traditional recruiting.

Beyond salaries and advertising spend, inefficiencies show up in:

Lost revenue from unfilled trucks
Increased accident risk from poor hiring decisions
Higher insurance premiums
Administrative overhead from managing multiple vendors

Platforms like Sentinel from Spotter AI are demonstrating that fleets can significantly reduce hiring-related costs while improving outcomes by eliminating redundant vendors and manual processes. Efficiency and safety are no longer trade-offs - they are aligned.

Technology Is Replacing Fragmentation

Historically, fleets have relied on a patchwork of tools and vendors to manage recruiting, compliance, and safety. This fragmented approach creates silos and slows decision-making.

Today, the trend is toward unified platforms that integrate hiring, screening, compliance, and monitoring into a single system.

Spotter AI is part of this shift, offering an approach that centralizes driver screening and verification into one streamlined platform rather than forcing fleets to juggle multiple systems.

These platforms connect with existing workflows, communication tools, and operational systems, enabling faster collaboration and better data visibility across the organization.

The Driver Experience Is Changing

Technology is not just transforming how fleets hire - it is also changing how drivers are evaluated and perceived.

As AI-driven scoring and verification become more common, transparency becomes critical. Drivers want to understand how they are being assessed and how their data is used.

Fleets that leverage platforms like Sentinel from Spotter AI while maintaining clear communication and fairness will have a competitive advantage in attracting and retaining drivers in a tight labor market.

Data Integrity Is the New Standard

One of the biggest challenges in traditional recruiting is reliance on self-reported information. Gaps in work history, inaccurate data, and inconsistent verification create risk.

Automated data collection and structured verification processes - like those built into Spotter AI's technology - eliminate much of this uncertainty.

By relying on verified, real-time data instead of manual inputs, fleets can make more confident hiring decisions and reduce exposure to fraud and compliance issues.

The trucking workforce is entering a new era where data, automation, and intelligence drive decision-making.

In the near future, we will see:

Fully automated hiring pipelines
Real-time driver scoring systems
Integration between recruiting, telematics, and safety platforms
Predictive models that forecast driver performance and risk

Fleets that continue to rely on manual, fragmented systems will struggle with slower hiring, higher costs, and increased risk.

Those that adopt AI-driven, data-centric approaches - including platforms like Sentinel from Spotter AI - will gain a clear advantage in speed, safety, compliance, and profitability.

The question is no longer whether the industry will change. It is how quickly fleets are willing to evolve.

North America Truck Sales Slump 13% in Q1 as Market Momentum Slows
2025-01-15
8 min read
TRUCK SALES
MARKET TRENDS
NORTH AMERICA

The North American heavy-duty truck market just posted its worst Q1 since the pandemic. Sales dropped 13% year-over-year-and the pain isn't isolated. From interest rates to tariffs, pressure is mounting on every side of the supply chain.

While global sales dipped across several key markets, the North American region is drawing particular attention due to its outsized role in global freight and its deeper exposure to economic headwinds.

"Tariff uncertainty and softening freight activity have pressured order intake and deliveries, especially in the U.S. market," Volvo Group noted in its Q1 2025 earnings release.

The decline reflects a cooling freight environment and increased caution among carriers and fleet operators - many of whom are postponing equipment purchases amid economic uncertainty, fluctuating diesel prices, and tighter credit conditions.

Q1 by the Numbers: A Deeper Look at North America

According to Q1 2025 data, 62,275 heavy-duty trucks were sold in North America - a significant drop from 71,329 units during the same period in 2024. This 13% decline represents more than 9,000 fewer trucks hitting the road in just the first quarter alone.
In response, the 2025 forecast for North American heavy-duty truck sales has been revised downward to 275,000 units, a 25,000-unit reduction compared to earlier estimates. This signals broader concern across OEMs and market analysts that softening demand may persist well into the second half of the year.

What's Fueling the Slowdown?

The North American trucking industry is navigating a complex set of challenges that are converging all at once:

Freight Recession & Spot Market Collapse
Rates are dipping below operating costs. Small carriers can't justify new investments.
Tariff & Trade Policy Whiplash
Uncertainty around global trade is freezing capital spending.
Financing Pressure from High Rates
With APRs above 8-9%, even well-run fleets are staying sidelined.
Regulatory Overhang
Pending GHG standards are adding another layer of hesitation.
North America in a Global Context

North America's slowdown isn't occurring in isolation. Global truck sales are seeing a general cooling trend, particularly in mature markets:

REGION	Q1 2025 SALES	Q1 2024 SALES	YOY CHANGE	FULL YEAR 2025 FORECAST	CHANGE VS. PREVIOUS FORECAST
North America	62,275	71,329	-13%	275,000	-25,000
Europe 30 (incl. UK)	70,142	82,530	-15%	290,000	Unchanged
China	213,408	222,454	-4%	710,000	Unchanged
India	105,851	103,695	+2%	380,000	+10,000

While India continues to see moderate growth driven by infrastructure expansion, North America and Europe are clearly in retrenchment mode.

Industry Implications

The Q1 numbers are more than just a reflection of economic sentiment - they signal a shift in how fleets are approaching growth, replacement cycles, and long-term planning.

OEMs like Volvo, Freightliner, and PACCAR may begin adjusting production levels to prevent inventory surpluses.
Aftermarket services and telematics platforms could see increased demand as fleets try to extend the life of existing vehicles.
Technology vendors in areas like dispatch automation, fuel efficiency, and driver safety could play a key role in helping fleets do more with less in 2025.
Looking Ahead

Despite the current slowdown, industry analysts expect a potential rebound in late 2025 or early 2026 - assuming interest rates begin to ease and regulatory clarity improves. The push toward electrification, automated dispatching, and predictive analytics is likely to accelerate once market confidence returns.
For now, however, the data paints a picture of strategic pause across the North American heavy-duty truck sector.

Class 8 Truck Orders Hit Post-Pandemic Low as Industry Faces Tariff Pressure and Market Uncertainty
2025-05-10
7 min read
CLASS 8 TRUCKS
ORDERS
TARIFFS
MARKET TRENDS

Class 8 truck orders just hit their lowest point since the early pandemic. With only 7,400-7,600 new trucks ordered in April, the industry is flashing warning lights-from tariffs to financing fatigue, uncertainty is steering the market into neutral.

Class 8 Orders Plunge

According to preliminary figures from both FTR Transportation Intelligence and ACT Research, net orders for North American Class 8 trucks in April 2025 came in at just:

FTR: 7,400 units (54% month-over-month and year-over-year)
ACT: 7,600 units, also reflecting sharp double-digit declines

These numbers are well below the 7-year April average of 18,963 units, and down 30% year-to-date compared to 2024.

"New and pending U.S. tariffs and retaliatory tariffs will significantly increase costs for Class 8 trucks, tractors, and related components," said FTR Senior Analyst Dan Moyer.

In the chart above, April's order volumes (shown in bright green) underscore how steep the drop-off has been compared to 2024 (blue line). It's a continuation of a downward trend that began in January and has yet to show signs of bottoming out.

Long-Term Order Trends: A Steady Decline

The second chart provides a broader perspective, showing Class 8 net orders from 2020 to April 2025. It's easy to spot the highs of post-COVID recovery in 2021 and 2022 - and the steady decline since late 2023. April's 7,600 units represent a 52% year-over-year drop, highlighting the industry's current volatility.

Even seasonally adjusted (SA) orders are tracking below 9,000 units, suggesting that fleet confidence is waning. And the issue isn't just declining orders - both ACT and FTR also report a recent spike in order cancellations, pointing to more than just caution… it's full-on hesitation.

5 Reasons Fleets Are Hitting Pause

Several overlapping forces are driving this downturn in new truck demand:

Tariff Tensions
Uncertainty around U.S. trade policies and potential retaliatory tariffs is spooking buyers. Many manufacturers expect part costs to rise sharply, which inflates final truck pricing and cuts into margins.
Used Truck Surplus
Used truck prices dropped sharply after peaking during COVID. With decent-condition models now more affordable, fleets are opting to delay purchases of new $180K-$200K trucks.
Backlogs & Delivery Delays
Order backlogs from 2022-2023 are still being worked through, meaning some carriers are still receiving trucks ordered 12-18 months ago, reducing urgency for new equipment.
Freight Market Weakness
Spot rates remain soft, and freight volumes have dipped across several sectors. Without strong market incentives, small and mid-sized carriers are hitting pause on capital spending.
Financing Fatigue
High interest rates are adding another layer of cost. For many operators, the monthly payment on a new truck just doesn't pencil out - especially if rates are upwards of 8-9%.
What's Next?

Short term? It's unlikely we'll see a major recovery before Q3 unless interest rates drop or trade policy stabilizes. Here's what analysts are watching:

Used truck prices are expected to stay flat or soften, especially as more inventory enters the market.
New truck prices may rise slightly due to parts inflation and regulatory compliance costs - though demand is keeping pricing pressure in check.
EPA 2027 regulations are on the horizon, and that could trigger a pre-buy boom if market confidence improves.

"With repair costs up, a weak resale market, and a murky tariff outlook, most carriers are playing it safe for now," said one ACT analyst.

Key Takeaways
April 2025 Class 8 orders dropped to ~7,600 units - lowest since May 2020
Down 54% YoY and MoM, with a 30% decline year-to-date
Order cancellations are rising, reflecting low fleet confidence
Used trucks remain attractive vs. new equipment
Tariffs, financing rates, and regulatory uncertainty continue to cloud forecasts

Fleet strategy in 2025 isn't about expansion-it's about positioning. The smart players aren't sitting idle; they're watching interest rates, holding cash, and prepping for a smarter Q3.
Want to lead that shift? Stay tuned-because the next freight upswing will reward those ready to move.

Dry Vans Are Struggling, But Flatbeds Are Heating Up

Dry vans are getting crushed. Rates are flat, demand is weak, and the short and long-term outlooks look uncertain. But one segment is standing tall-open deck freight.

Long-Term Market Momentum

Q1 Performance: Best in Years

Spot rates for flatbeds climbed from $2.44 in February to $2.57 in April, a +1.6% YoY increase. That makes Q1 2025 the strongest flatbed rate environment since 2017.

Stockpiling in response to tariff uncertainty

Reactivating dormant domestic production lines

While challenges exist, flatbed is in a much better position than dry van or reefer. It's closely tied to infrastructure, energy, and domestic production-all priorities under a Trump policy agenda.

As tariffs rise, re-shoring continues, and construction accelerates, open-deck freight could not only survive but lead the recovery.

Flatbed is hot-and it may just stay that way.

FREIGHT

International Shipping Surge

A 90-day tariff truce between the U.S. and China, effective May 12, 2025, is already shaking up global logistics. Importers are rushing to capitalize on the policy window, sparking a sharp spike in ocean volumes and container rates.
This isn't business as usual-it's a signal that peak season may come earlier and hotter than expected.

Ocean Shipping Rebounds on Tariff Pause

Rate Jumps:

20-ft containers (Shanghai to Long Beach): $2,300 (up 27.8% from April)
40-ft containers: $2,900 (up 31.8% )

Shippers are racing to move goods ahead of potential policy reversals. Carriers are tightening space and raising rates in response.

Diversifying Gateways

While China still leads as the largest source of inbound TEUs to the U.S., volumes have dropped significantly YoY. Meanwhile, other countries are gaining ground:

Thailand: +55.35% YoY
Vietnam: +27.59% YoY
Germany: +22.84% YoY

These shifts signal broader diversification in sourcing beyond China-a trend accelerated by trade friction and supply chain resilience planning.

Trucking Ripple Effect

Ocean transit times average ~30 days, meaning the trucking sector will start to feel the effects by early July-right in time for the 4th of July freight peak. Brokers and carriers should expect rate pressure and tighter capacity just as summer promotions hit full swing.

Class 8 Truck Orders Hit a Wall

While ocean freight surges, new truck orders continue their dramatic fall. April was particularly harsh:

New truck orders: 7,400 units (down 54% YoY)
Sales: 18,078 units (down 8.7% YoY)
Freightliner: Maintains 36.2% market share, outperforming competitors

OEMs are pumping the brakes as demand cools.

Used Market Snapshot

On the flip side, the used truck market is showing mixed signals:

Retail sales: +8.6% MoM
Auction sales: -57%

While some fleets are still buying, many are holding off or opting for the secondary market instead of investing in new equipment.

Trailer Orders Defy the Trend

March saw strong performance in the trailer sector, bucking the downward trend in tractors:

~21,200 units ordered
+21% MoM | +63% YoY

This indicates fleets are expanding trailer capacity, either for drop-and-hook operations or to handle seasonal freight surges without committing to new drivers or power units.

Freight Rate Outlook: Capacity Tightens Ahead of Peak

As produce season takes hold, freight rates are climbing steadily. The National Truckload Index (NTI) is holding at $2.23/mi and trending upward.

Rejections Signal Spot Market Pressure

The Van Outbound Tender Rejection Index (VOTRI) is also rising, now at 5.44-well above this time in 2022 and 2023. This means contracted carriers are rejecting more freight, pushing volume into the spot market.

Higher rejections = tighter capacity = potential for sustained rate spikes through the summer.

Southern Produce Is Powering Regional Markets

Southern U.S. regions are heating up with seasonal produce freight. Melons, in particular, are showing strong activity:

100+ active loads
~$300,000 in gross revenue

This is driving a localized boom in reefer and dry van markets across Texas, Georgia, and Florida. Regional carriers are taking advantage of short-haul, high-yield lanes.

Bonus Insight: Mode Share and Market Activity

New visual data reveals further insight into freight movement by mode and region. This snapshot gives a clear breakdown of truckload, intermodal, and LTL market share trends. For brokers and shippers, this type of breakdown is essential in identifying which freight paths are growing more competitive.

This data supports the broader trend: truckload activity is trending upward, while intermodal has flattened out, signaling a continued preference for flexible OTR options during periods of high demand.

May is proving to be a turning point month: international freight is heating up, domestic equipment sales are cooling, and summer peak season is on the horizon.

What to Watch:
Continued rise in ocean TEUs arriving in late June
Spot rate pressure increasing across major van lanes
Trailer demand holding steady despite OEM slowdowns
Southern produce volumes boosting localized freight markets

May is more than a warm-up-it's a signal flare. Ocean rates are up, trailers are moving, and tender rejections are climbing. Carriers who act early will ride the July wave. The rest? They'll be playing catch-up.
Plan now. Scale smart. And stay ahead of the freight curve.

What the Latest Driver Demographics Report Means for Fleets
2025-07-30
6 min read
DRIVER DEMOGRAPHICS
ATRI
RECRUITING
OWNER-OPERATORS
DIVERSITY

ATRI has just released its highly anticipated 2025 update on truck driver demographics-and it's a must-read for anyone recruiting or retaining drivers in today's shifting workforce. This report doesn't just outline how many drivers are out there. It reveals who they are, how they're changing, and what fleets need to adapt to in order to stay competitive.

1. How Many Drivers Are in the Market?

As of 2023, there were 3.55 million truck drivers in the U.S., and the number continues to climb steadily.

Of those drivers, nearly 58% operate tractor-trailers, with the rest working in regional, local, or last-mile delivery.

2. The Industry Is Aging-Fast

The average age of a truck driver today is 47 years old. Only 20.4% of drivers are under 35, vs. 35% in the overall U.S. labor force. That means fleets are competing for a shrinking pool of younger talent.

3. Younger Women Are Entering the Industry-Later

The share of women in trucking is still stuck at ~4%. But there's a key insight: women tend to enter the industry later, with a median entry age of 40, compared to 26 for men. If you want to engage women in trucking, marketing to second‑career professionals may be the key.

4. The Rise of Owner-Operators

The growth of single-truck fleets continues. Today, 54.4% of fleets operate just one truck. This is huge for lease‑purchase programs and independent contractor models-CDL holders are increasingly choosing independence.

5. The Industry Is Becoming More Diverse

In the last decade:

White driver representation has fallen from 77% to 63%
Hispanic and Black driver shares have each risen to 23%

Fleets must consider how culture, language, and regional recruiting strategies can improve retention across a more diverse workforce.

6. Hiring Individuals with Criminal Records

Fleets are increasingly open to second‑chance hiring, but thresholds still matter. Here's a quick breakdown of carrier suitability based on the type and timing of conviction:

OFFENSE TYPE	0-5 YEARS	5-10 YEARS	10+ YEARS
Violent Felony	Not Suitable	Proceed w/ Caution	Proceed w/ Caution
Sexual Conviction	Not Suitable	Not Suitable	Proceed w/ Caution
Fraud/Theft	Not Suitable	Viable Consideration	Viable Consideration
DUI/DWI	Not Suitable	Viable Consideration	Viable Consideration

This table shows a growing openness in the industry-but time and offense type still play a key role in eligibility.

Final Thoughts: What This Means for Fleets
The driver pool is aging.
Younger drivers and women are underrepresented.
Single‑truck fleets and diverse ownership are on the rise.
Fleets willing to adapt hiring standards (within reason) may tap into overlooked talent.

If you're building driver programs or shaping your employer brand, understanding these shifts isn't optional-it's strategic.

Trailer Orders Surge in June, But Long-Term Weakness Remains
2025-07-29
5 min read
TRAILERS
ORDERS
ACT RESEARCH
MARKET TRENDS

June 2025 brought a much-needed jolt to the trailer market. Net orders for trailers jumped to nearly 15,400 units, more than double May's total and 24% higher than June 2024. But while the headline looks promising, industry insiders urge caution before calling this a true recovery.

Short-Term Lift or Strategic Move?

Analysts at ACT Research believe this spike is less about market recovery and more about fleets pulling orders forward to lock in current pricing before anticipated cost increases. In short, fleets are planning ahead-not expanding aggressively.

"This looks like a strategic play, not a sign of surging demand," said one ACT analyst. "Fleets know higher prices are coming, and they're securing units early."

Still Lagging Long-Term Averages

Despite June's bounce, total trailer demand remains well below pre-2023 levels. The chart above shows how net orders have fluctuated over the past nine years-and 2024 and 2025 remain among the softest periods since the pandemic.

Adding to the caution: cancellation rates ticked up again, signaling uncertainty across the market. Buyers who rushed in last year may now be backtracking due to shifting freight volumes, tight margins, or concerns about overcapacity.

Outlook for the Rest of 2025

Even with June's rebound, the overall outlook remains cautious:

Q3 trailer orders are expected to moderate as early buys taper off
Cancellation trends will be closely watched as a proxy for carrier sentiment
OEM backlogs are still being worked through, but 2026 visibility remains unclear
Freight demand softness may continue to put pressure on capital expenditures
What It Means for Buyers

If you're considering trailer purchases for Q4 or early 2026, this is a moment of leverage. Fleets that act early may secure favorable terms before pricing pressure returns. But for now, June's data looks more like a strategic reshuffling than the start of a full market rebound.

What is a Bobtail Truck? Definition, Risks & Driving Tips
April 14, 2026
7 min read
BOBTAIL TRUCK
TRUCKING BASICS
FLEET SAFETY
CDL DRIVERS
TRUCKING TERMS

If you have ever seen a semi-truck cab driving down the highway without a trailer attached, you have seen a bobtail truck in action. It is one of the most common sights in trucking, yet many drivers, shippers, and fleet managers do not fully understand what it means, why it happens, or why it carries unique risks that fleets need to manage carefully.

This guide covers everything you need to know about bobtail trucks - from the origin of the term to the safety considerations that every CDL driver and fleet operator should be aware of.

What Does Bobtail Mean in Trucking?

In trucking, bobtail refers to a semi-truck (also called a tractor) that is operating without a trailer. When a truck is bobtailing, the tractor unit is driving on its own, disconnected from any load or trailer. This is the opposite of how a semi-truck is designed to operate - the standard configuration is a tractor pulling a loaded or empty trailer.

The term comes from the "Bob-tail" cat breed known for its short tail, or more likely from old American folk songs about horses pulling sleighs. In trucking culture, the word has been used for decades to describe a cab-only truck run.

Why Do Truck Drivers Drive Bobtail?

Bobtailing is a normal and necessary part of trucking operations. Drivers and fleets bobtail for several legitimate reasons:

Picking up a new trailer: A driver drops off a loaded trailer at a destination and then drives bobtail to the next pickup location to hook up a new load.
Returning to a terminal: After delivering a trailer, drivers often return to their home base or a drop yard without a trailer attached.
Repositioning the tractor: Fleets sometimes need to move tractors from one yard to another without a trailer available.
Maintenance and repairs: Trucks going in for service often travel bobtail to and from the shop.
Deadhead trips: When no backhaul load is available, a driver may need to reposition bobtail.
Is Bobtail Driving More Dangerous?

Yes - and this is the most important thing fleet managers and drivers need to understand. Bobtail trucks are significantly more difficult to control than a fully loaded truck-trailer combination. This is counterintuitive to many people, but the physics explain it clearly:

Reduced Traction on the Drive Axles

A fully loaded trailer pushes down on the tractor's fifth wheel, which transfers weight onto the drive axles. This weight is what gives the drive tires traction. When a tractor is bobtailing, there is no trailer weight pressing down - the rear drive axles carry far less weight. This dramatically reduces traction, especially in wet, icy, or loose road conditions.

Braking Distance is Much Longer

Commercial truck brakes are engineered to stop a fully loaded combination vehicle. When applied to a light bobtail tractor, these powerful brakes can cause the rear wheels to lock up and the truck to skid. Stopping distances for a bobtail truck in wet conditions can be 40% longer than most drivers expect.

Stiffer Ride and Less Stability

The air suspension and spring system on a semi-truck is designed to absorb load weight. Without a trailer, the rear of the tractor bounces much more aggressively over road imperfections. This makes the truck feel unstable and reduces the driver's ability to maintain precise control.

Risk of Jackknifing

While jackknifing is typically associated with truck-trailer combos, bobtail tractors can experience a similar loss of directional control when the rear axles lose traction during hard braking - especially on slick surfaces.

Bobtail Safety Tips for CDL Drivers

Experienced drivers know to adjust their driving technique significantly when operating bobtail. Here are the key practices every driver should follow:

Brake early and gently. Apply brakes gradually and well in advance of stops. Hard braking is dangerous when bobtail. Give yourself twice the normal stopping distance.
Slow down in adverse weather. Rain, ice, and snow amplify every bobtail handling challenge. Reduce speed significantly and increase following distance.
Take turns wider and slower. The truck handles differently without a trailer. Corners and on-ramps feel sharper and less predictable.
Watch for wind. Bobtail tractors have a high profile with no trailer weight to stabilize them. Crosswinds can push the truck off course more easily.
Use engine braking carefully. Engine braking (jake brake) can cause the rear wheels to lock in slippery conditions when bobtail. Use it lightly or not at all on wet roads.
Pre-trip inspection still applies. Just because there is no trailer does not mean the inspection can be skipped. Lights, brakes, tires, and fluid levels must all be checked.
Bobtail vs. Deadhead: What is the Difference?

These two terms are often confused but they mean different things:

TERM	DEFINITION	WHAT IS BEING MOVED
Bobtail	Tractor driving without any trailer	Tractor only
Deadhead	Tractor pulling an empty trailer	Tractor + empty trailer

Deadheading is actually safer than bobtailing because the empty trailer adds weight and stability to the drive axles, improving traction and brake effectiveness.

Bobtail Insurance: What Fleets Need to Know

Standard trucking liability policies (motor carrier policies) cover a truck when it is under dispatch - meaning operating with a load. When a driver is bobtailing between jobs, they may not be covered by the carrier's primary policy. This creates a coverage gap that can expose both the driver and the fleet to serious financial risk.

Bobtail insurance (also called non-trucking liability or deadhead insurance) is a separate policy that covers the tractor when it is operated outside of dispatch - including bobtail and personal use. Owner-operators leasing to carriers are especially likely to need this coverage, as the carrier's insurance typically only applies when the truck is under their dispatch.

Key points about bobtail insurance:

It covers liability for accidents that occur while bobtailing (not under dispatch)
It does not cover the truck itself (that requires physical damage coverage)
It is typically inexpensive - often $30–$50 per month for owner-operators
Fleets should confirm whether their primary policy extends to bobtail operations
How Fleet Management Software Tracks Bobtail Operations

Modern fleet management platforms like Spotter TMS give fleet managers real-time visibility into every tractor in their fleet - including when and where trucks are operating bobtail. This matters for several reasons:

Safety monitoring: Knowing when drivers are running bobtail allows dispatchers to flag higher-risk segments and ensure drivers are following safe bobtail procedures.
Insurance compliance: Tracking bobtail miles separately from loaded miles helps ensure correct insurance coverage is in place and simplifies claims management.
Efficiency analysis: Excessive bobtail miles signal dispatch inefficiencies - loads and trailers are not being positioned well. A good TMS helps minimize unproductive bobtail trips.
DOT compliance: Hours of service rules apply whether a driver is loaded or bobtail. Accurate ELD tracking ensures compliance regardless of load status.
Frequently Asked Questions About Bobtail Trucks
Can a bobtail truck carry cargo?

No. A bobtail truck is specifically a tractor operating without a trailer. It cannot carry freight. Any cargo would require a trailer to be attached.

Is bobtailing illegal?

Bobtailing is completely legal. It is a normal part of trucking operations. However, drivers must maintain their CDL and follow all applicable traffic laws and HOS regulations while operating bobtail.

Why is bobtail insurance separate from regular trucking insurance?

Standard motor carrier policies cover trucks under dispatch (carrying loads). Bobtail operations fall outside that scope, creating a liability gap. Bobtail insurance fills that gap for operations between loads.

Does FMCSA regulate bobtail operations?

Yes. FMCSA regulations apply to commercial motor vehicle operators regardless of whether they are hauling a load. Hours of service, vehicle inspection requirements, and CDL rules all apply during bobtail operations.

What is a straight truck vs. a bobtail truck?

A straight truck (also called a box truck or single-unit truck) is a truck where the cab and cargo area are on the same frame. A bobtail truck specifically refers to a semi-truck tractor operating without its trailer - these are two different types of vehicles.

What is GVWR? Gross Vehicle Weight Rating Explained for Trucks & Fleets
April 14, 2026
9 min read
GVWR
TRUCKING COMPLIANCE
COMMERCIAL VEHICLES
FLEET MANAGEMENT
DOT REGULATIONS

If you operate commercial trucks, manage a fleet, or are working toward your CDL, you will encounter the term GVWR constantly. It appears on vehicle registration, DOT compliance checks, bridge laws, and insurance documents. Yet despite how frequently it comes up, many drivers and fleet managers do not have a complete understanding of what it means and why it matters.

This guide explains GVWR in plain language - what it is, how it is calculated, how it differs from related terms like GVW and GCWR, and why it is one of the most important numbers in commercial trucking compliance.

What is GVWR?

GVWR stands for Gross Vehicle Weight Rating. It is the maximum total weight that a vehicle manufacturer certifies the vehicle can safely carry. This includes:

The weight of the vehicle itself (curb weight)
The weight of all passengers and the driver
The weight of all cargo and payload
The weight of fuel and fluids
The weight of any permanently attached equipment

GVWR is set by the vehicle manufacturer and is listed on the vehicle's door jamb sticker, title, and registration. It is a rating - a maximum limit - not the actual weight of the vehicle at any given moment.

GVWR vs GVW: What is the Difference?

This is one of the most common points of confusion in trucking:

TERM	WHAT IT MEANS	WHO SETS IT
GVWR (Gross Vehicle Weight Rating)	The maximum weight the vehicle is rated to carry - a fixed limit	Vehicle manufacturer
GVW (Gross Vehicle Weight)	The actual weight of the vehicle at a specific moment - varies by load	Measured at a weigh station

Your GVWR never changes - it is stamped by the manufacturer. Your GVW changes every trip depending on how much cargo you are hauling. For legal operation, your GVW must never exceed your GVWR.

GVWR vs GCWR: Combinations and Trailers

When a truck is pulling a trailer, a third term becomes relevant:

GCWR (Gross Combined Weight Rating): The maximum total weight of a truck and its trailer combined, as rated by the manufacturer. This applies to tractor-trailer combinations.
The GVWR applies to each vehicle individually (the tractor has its own GVWR; the trailer has its own GVWR).
The GCWR is the combined maximum for both together.
GVWR Truck Classes: The Full Breakdown

The federal government and the trucking industry use GVWR to classify trucks into categories. This classification determines licensing requirements, DOT regulations, insurance rates, and more.

CLASS	GVWR RANGE	TYPICAL VEHICLES	LICENSE REQUIRED
Class 1	0 – 6,000 lbs	Small pickups, minivans	Regular driver's license
Class 2	6,001 – 10,000 lbs	Full-size pickups, cargo vans	Regular driver's license
Class 3	10,001 – 14,000 lbs	Large pickups, walk-in vans	Regular (some states require CDL)
Class 4	14,001 – 16,000 lbs	City delivery trucks	CDL may be required
Class 5	16,001 – 19,500 lbs	Bucket trucks, large delivery	CDL may be required
Class 6	19,501 – 26,000 lbs	Beverage trucks, school buses	CDL required over 26,001 lbs
Class 7	26,001 – 33,000 lbs	City transit buses, garbage trucks	CDL required
Class 8	33,001 lbs and above	Semi-trucks, heavy haul	CDL required

The 26,001 lb GVWR threshold is one of the most important numbers in trucking because it is the point at which federal CDL requirements kick in under FMCSA regulations.

Why GVWR Matters for DOT Compliance

The GVWR of your vehicle determines which federal and state regulations apply to your operation. Here is why fleet managers need to pay close attention:

CDL Requirements

Any single vehicle with a GVWR over 26,000 lbs, or any combination vehicle with a GCWR over 26,000 lbs (where the trailer's GVWR exceeds 10,000 lbs), requires the driver to hold a valid Commercial Driver's License (CDL). Fleets operating vehicles near this threshold must verify their driver's licensing carefully.

FMCSA Hours of Service

FMCSA HOS regulations apply to commercial motor vehicles with a GVWR of 10,001 lbs or more operating in interstate commerce. Fleets operating vehicles in this range must use ELD-compliant logging devices and comply with all driver rest requirements.

DOT Number and Registration

Vehicles with a GVWR over 10,001 lbs operating in interstate commerce must be registered with the FMCSA and display a USDOT number. Fleets that add or replace vehicles must ensure new equipment is properly registered based on its GVWR.

Bridge Laws and Weight Permits

State bridge laws restrict vehicle weights on public roads to protect infrastructure. These laws are tied directly to axle weights and GVW - which must stay below GVWR. Overweight violations are expensive and can result in out-of-service orders during roadside inspections.

Weigh Station Requirements

Trucks with a GVWR over 10,000 lbs are generally required to stop at weigh stations. Officers check that the actual GVW does not exceed the vehicle's GVWR and applicable state weight limits.

How Exceeding GVWR Affects Your Fleet

Running a truck over its GVWR is not just a compliance issue - it creates real operational and safety risks:

Accelerated wear: Overloading stresses the frame, suspension, tires, and brakes beyond their design limits, leading to premature failure and higher maintenance costs.
Increased stopping distance: Overloaded trucks take significantly longer to stop, increasing accident risk.
Voided warranties: Operating over GVWR can void manufacturer warranties on affected components.
Insurance implications: Claims involving an overloaded vehicle can be denied or reduced by insurers.
Fines and citations: Overweight violations at weigh stations carry fines that can run hundreds to thousands of dollars per incident.
How Fleet Management Software Tracks GVWR Compliance

Fleet management platforms like Spotter TMS help fleets stay ahead of GVWR-related compliance issues by:

Maintaining a digital record of each vehicle's GVWR alongside its registration and inspection history
Flagging vehicles when payload assignments approach or exceed rated limits
Alerting managers when driver licenses do not match the GVWR class of assigned vehicles
Integrating with DOT compliance workflows to simplify audit preparation
Tracking maintenance schedules that account for actual load weights over time
Frequently Asked Questions About GVWR
Can I increase my truck's GVWR?

No. GVWR is a manufacturer-rated maximum and cannot be increased by an operator. Upgrades to suspension, axles, or tires do not change the GVWR stamped on the vehicle - they may improve performance but the legal GVWR remains fixed by the OEM.

Where do I find my truck's GVWR?

GVWR is printed on the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) compliance sticker, usually located on the driver's door jamb. It is also listed on the vehicle title, registration, and manufacturer's spec sheet.

Does GVWR include the weight of the driver?

Yes. GVWR represents the maximum total weight the vehicle can carry - including the driver, all passengers, cargo, fuel, and all fluids.

What happens if I get caught exceeding GVWR?

You can be cited for an overweight violation, fined, and potentially placed out of service until the load is redistributed or reduced. Repeat violations can result in elevated FMCSA safety scores and increased insurance premiums.

Is GVWR the same as payload capacity?

No. Payload capacity is calculated as GVWR minus the vehicle's curb weight (the weight of the empty vehicle). GVWR is the total maximum; payload is the remaining margin available for cargo and passengers.

ELD Trucking: Complete Guide to Electronic Logging Devices
April 14, 2026
9 min read
ELD
ELECTRONIC LOGS
HOURS OF SERVICE
DOT COMPLIANCE
FLEET MANAGEMENT
CDL DRIVERS

If you operate commercial trucks or manage a fleet, ELDs are non-negotiable. The Electronic Logging Device mandate changed how the entire industry tracks driver hours - replacing paper logs with tamper-resistant digital records tied directly to a vehicle's engine. Whether you are a fleet manager selecting devices, a CDL driver learning the system, or a carrier working through compliance, this guide covers everything you need to know.

What is an ELD (Electronic Logging Device)?

An Electronic Logging Device (ELD) is a hardware device that connects to a commercial motor vehicle's engine control module (ECM) and automatically records the driver's Hours of Service (HOS) data. The device captures when the engine is running, the vehicle's movement, and which duty status the driver has selected - eliminating manual paper logbook entries.

ELDs synchronize with a mobile app or tablet display so the driver can view their log, switch duty statuses, and certify their record at the end of each shift. The data is stored in a standardized format that can be transferred wirelessly to DOT enforcement officers during roadside inspections.

The ELD Mandate - What It Is and When It Took Effect

The FMCSA ELD Mandate (49 CFR Part 395) was published in December 2015 and phased in over several years:

December 18, 2017: Full compliance required for most carriers - paper logs were no longer permitted for covered drivers.
December 16, 2019: Grandfathering period for AOBRDs ended. All AOBRDs had to be replaced with FMCSA-registered ELDs.
Who is Required to Use an ELD?

The ELD mandate applies to commercial motor vehicle (CMV) drivers who are required to keep Records of Duty Status (RODS) under FMCSA Hours of Service rules. Exemptions include: the short-haul exemption (150 air-mile radius), driveaway-towaway operations, pre-2000 engine vehicles, the 8-day paper log rule, and certain agricultural operations.

How ELDs Work - What Data They Capture

An ELD connects directly to the vehicle's ECM and automatically records engine hours, vehicle miles, date and time (UTC-synchronized), GPS location, driver identification, duty status changes, unidentified driving periods, and malfunctions. The data is stored on the device and can be transmitted via Bluetooth, USB, or wireless transfer to enforcement officers during inspections. Carriers must retain ELD records for a minimum of six months.

Hours of Service Rules That ELDs Enforce
RULE	LIMIT	DESCRIPTION
11-Hour Driving Limit	11 hours	Maximum driving after 10 consecutive hours off duty
14-Hour On-Duty Window	14 hours	Cannot drive beyond the 14th consecutive on-duty hour
30-Minute Break	30 min after 8 hours	Required break after 8 cumulative hours of driving
70-Hour / 8-Day Limit	70 hours in 8 days	Cannot drive after 70 on-duty hours in 8 consecutive days
34-Hour Restart	34 consecutive hours	Restarts the 60/70-hour clock
Common ELD Violations and Fines
VIOLATION	POTENTIAL FINE
No ELD / ELD not in use	Up to $16,000 per violation
ELD malfunction not reported	Up to $1,270 per day
Failure to transfer data to enforcement	Out-of-service order; up to $1,270
HOS violation - driving over 11 hours	$1,000–$16,000 per violation
False logs / log manipulation	Up to $16,000; potential criminal charges
How Spotter TMS Integrates with ELD Data for Full Fleet Visibility

Spotter TMS integrates with ELD data to give fleet managers a unified view: real-time HOS visibility for every driver, automated compliance alerts before violations occur, driver performance tracking, maintenance scheduling aligned with engine hours, audit-ready record keeping, and load-driver matching based on actual HOS status.

Frequently Asked Questions About ELD Trucking
What happens if my ELD malfunctions during a trip?

Note the malfunction code, notify your carrier within 24 hours, and revert to paper logs for up to 8 days while the device is repaired or replaced. Carry the paper logs and a written statement of the malfunction during any inspection.

Can a driver edit entries on an ELD?

Drivers can edit certain fields and add annotations, but the original automated record is always preserved alongside any edits, creating an audit trail. No edit can remove the underlying engine-synchronized data.

Do owner-operators need an ELD?

Yes, if you operate a CMV in interstate commerce and are required to keep Records of Duty Status. The mandate applies equally to single-truck owner-operators and large fleets.

How long must ELD records be kept?

FMCSA regulations require carriers to retain ELD records for a minimum of six months. Drivers must have access to the previous 7 days of logs on the device during any trip.

DOT Inspection Checklist: Complete Guide for Truck Drivers and Fleet Managers
April 14, 2026
10 min read
DOT INSPECTION
DOT COMPLIANCE
FLEET SAFETY
CSA SCORE
FMCSA

Roadside DOT inspections are one of the most consequential events in a truck driver's workday. A single out-of-service violation can sideline a driver for hours, damage your fleet's CSA score, trigger follow-up audits, and cost thousands in lost revenue. Yet most violations that cause these outcomes are entirely preventable - they come down to maintenance gaps and documentation failures that a prepared fleet can eliminate.

This guide covers every level of DOT inspection, exactly what inspectors check at each level, the violations most likely to put a truck out of service, how your drivers should prepare, and how your CSA score is affected by inspection outcomes.

What Is a DOT Inspection?

A DOT inspection (also called a roadside inspection or CVSA inspection) is a physical examination of a commercial motor vehicle and its driver, conducted by law enforcement officers or certified inspectors at weigh stations, roadside checkpoints, or during traffic enforcement stops. These inspections are governed by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) and carried out under standards set by the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance (CVSA).

Inspections verify that commercial vehicles and their drivers comply with federal safety regulations. The results are recorded in the FMCSA's Motor Carrier Management Information System (MCMIS) and used to calculate your fleet's CSA (Compliance, Safety, Accountability) score - a score that directly affects your ability to win freight contracts and avoid federal audits.

The 7 Levels of DOT Inspection
LEVEL	NAME	WHAT IS INSPECTED	WHO PERFORMS IT
Level I	North American Standard Inspection	Full driver and vehicle inspection - the most comprehensive level	Certified roadside inspector
Level II	Walk-Around Driver / Vehicle Inspection	All Level I items that can be checked without going under the vehicle	Certified roadside inspector
Level III	Driver-Only Inspection	Driver credentials, HOS logs, medical certificate, seatbelt - no vehicle check	Certified inspector or law enforcement
Level IV	Special Study Inspection	One-time data collection on specific items for research purposes	Certified inspector
Level V	Vehicle-Only Inspection	Full vehicle inspection without the driver present	Certified inspector
Level VI	Enhanced NAS Inspection for Radioactive Shipments	Level I inspection plus radiological checks for hazmat loads	Specially trained inspector
Level VII	Comprehensive Truck Size and Weight	Weight, dimensions, and permit compliance - often at weigh stations	State enforcement officer
What Inspectors Check: The Full DOT Inspection Checklist
Brakes
Brake adjustment on all axles (slack adjusters, push rod travel)
Brake lining and pad thickness - worn below minimums is an immediate OOS violation
Brake hoses and tubing - cracks, chafing, or leaks
Air system pressure and leakage rate
Spring brakes and parking brake function
Anti-lock braking system (ABS) warning light functionality
Brake drums and rotors for cracks or heat damage
Tires
Tread depth - steer tires require minimum 4/32", all other positions require 2/32"
Tire pressure - significantly under-inflated tires are an OOS violation
Sidewall condition - cuts, bulges, or exposed cords
Flat or leaking tires
Tires making contact with any part of the vehicle
Mismatched tire sizes on the same axle
Lights and Electrical
Headlights (high and low beam)
Tail lights, brake lights, and reverse lights
Turn signals (front and rear)
Hazard lights
Clearance, marker, and identification lights
Reflectors - required at specific positions on the vehicle
ABS malfunction indicator lamp
Steering and Suspension
Steering wheel free play - excessive play is an OOS condition
Steering gear box for secure mounting and leaks
Tie rods, drag links, and steering arms for wear or damage
Power steering fluid level and hose condition
Leaf springs - broken or missing leaves
Air suspension components - bags, lines, mounting hardware
U-bolts and spring hangers for secure mounting
Coupling Devices
Fifth wheel - must be properly latched, no visible play when tested
Kingpin - inspected for wear or damage
Safety chains and cables
Glad hands and air lines between tractor and trailer
Landing gear - fully retracted and secure
Emergency Equipment
Fire extinguisher - properly charged, correct rating (5 B:C minimum)
Three bidirectional emergency reflective triangles (or equivalent flares/fuses)
Spare fuses (if the vehicle uses fuses)
Driver Documents (Level I and Level III)
Commercial Driver's License (CDL) - valid, correct class, correct endorsements for load type
Medical Examiner's Certificate - current and not expired
Hours of Service records - ELD or paper logs, with 8 days of prior records available
Bill of Lading - matching the cargo being carried
Annual vehicle inspection report - must be in the cab and current
IRP cab card - vehicle registration for the correct jurisdiction
Common Violations That Cause Out-of-Service Orders
Vehicle Out-of-Service Violations
Brake adjustment out of spec - the leading cause of vehicle OOS orders year after year
Brake hose or tubing damage - cracked, abraded, or leaking air lines
Tire tread below minimum depth - especially on steer tires
Flat or underinflated tires
Inoperative required lights - brake lights and headlights are most critical
Unsecured or improperly secured cargo
Broken or missing leaf springs
Driver Out-of-Service Violations
Hours of service violation - driving beyond legal limits or falsifying logs
No valid CDL or wrong endorsement for the cargo type
Expired medical certificate
ELD malfunction without compliant paper log backup
How to Prepare Your Drivers and Fleet for DOT Inspections
Daily Pre-Trip Inspections

FMCSA requires drivers to complete a pre-trip inspection before each shift and a post-trip inspection at the end of each day. Train drivers to actually check brake adjustment, tire condition, all required lights, coupling security, and emergency equipment - not just walk around the truck checking boxes.

Preventive Maintenance Scheduling

Brake adjusters, tire wear, and lighting failures are all predictable, time-based failures. A disciplined preventive maintenance (PM) schedule that pulls trucks for brake service, tire rotation, and lighting inspection before these items reach OOS thresholds will dramatically reduce your inspection violation rate.

ELD Compliance and HOS Training

Hours of service violations are one of the most common driver OOS causes. Ensure every driver knows how to operate the ELD correctly, understands the current HOS rules (the 11-hour driving limit, 14-hour on-duty window, 30-minute rest break requirement, and 70-hour cycle), and knows what to do if the ELD malfunctions during a trip.

How DOT Inspections Affect Your CSA Score

The CSA program is the FMCSA's system for measuring carrier safety performance. Your CSA score is calculated using data from roadside inspections, crash reports, and investigation findings - and it directly determines whether your carrier receives increased scrutiny from FMCSA, up to and including compliance reviews (audits).

CSA groups violations into seven Behavior Analysis and Safety Improvement Categories (BASICs): Unsafe Driving, Hours of Service Compliance, Driver Fitness, Controlled Substances and Alcohol, Vehicle Maintenance, Hazardous Materials Compliance, and Crash Indicator.

Clean inspections are one of the most effective tools for managing your CSA score. Each clean inspection adds a data point that, when aggregated, pushes your percentile down relative to carriers with violations.

How Fleet Management Software Helps You Manage Inspection Records

Spotter TMS gives fleet managers a centralized compliance dashboard that tracks every vehicle's inspection history, PM schedule, and documentation status in one place. Key capabilities include annual inspection tracking, DVIR management, preventive maintenance scheduling, document storage, CSA score monitoring, and inspection readiness reports.

The fleets with the best CSA scores are not the ones that react to roadside inspections - they are the ones that have built compliance into their daily operating rhythm.

What is LTL Freight? Less Than Truckload Shipping Explained
April 14, 2026
8 min read
LTL
LESS THAN TRUCKLOAD
FREIGHT SHIPPING
TRUCKING BASICS
LOGISTICS

LTL (Less Than Truckload) freight is one of the most common shipping methods in North America. Whether you are a shipper trying to reduce freight costs, a carrier looking to maximize revenue per load, or a logistics manager building a transportation strategy, this guide covers everything you need to know about LTL freight.

What is LTL (Less Than Truckload) Freight?

LTL freight refers to shipments that do not require a full truckload. Instead of one shipper filling an entire trailer, multiple shippers share space on the same truck. Each shipper pays only for the portion of the truck their freight occupies. A typical LTL shipment ranges from 150 lbs to 15,000 lbs and occupies between 1 and 6 pallets.

How LTL Shipping Works
Pickup: The LTL carrier dispatches a local pickup truck to collect your freight, consolidating multiple pickups efficiently.
Origin Terminal: Freight arrives at the carrier's local service center, sorted by destination and consolidated with other shipments.
Line-Haul: Consolidated freight moves on a long-haul trailer between service centers.
Destination Terminal: Freight is sorted and loaded onto a local delivery vehicle.
Delivery: A local driver makes final-mile delivery to the consignee.
LTL vs FTL: Key Differences
FACTOR	LTL (LESS THAN TRUCKLOAD)	FTL (FULL TRUCKLOAD)
Shipment Size	150 lbs – 15,000 lbs (1–6 pallets)	10,000 lbs+ (7–30+ pallets)
Cost Structure	Pay only for space used; shared cost	Pay for full trailer regardless of fill
Transit Time	Longer; multiple stops and terminals	Faster; direct point-to-point
Freight Handling	Multiple touch points; higher damage risk	Minimal handling; lower damage risk
Best For	Small-to-medium shipments, cost-sensitive freight	Large shipments, fragile or time-critical freight
LTL Freight Classes (NMFC Classification)

Every LTL shipment is assigned a freight class under the National Motor Freight Classification (NMFC) system. There are 18 freight classes ranging from Class 50 (densest, cheapest) to Class 500 (lowest density, most expensive). Class is determined by density, stowability, handling difficulty, and liability.

NMFC CLASS	DENSITY (LBS/CUBIC FT)	TYPICAL COMMODITIES
Class 50	50+ lbs/cu ft	Heavy machinery parts, steel bolts, sand
Class 70	15–22.5 lbs/cu ft	Auto engines, food items, unassembled furniture
Class 100	9–10.5 lbs/cu ft	Wine, caskets, car covers
Class 150	6–7 lbs/cu ft	Auto sheet metal, motorcycles
Class 250	3–4 lbs/cu ft	Bamboo furniture, mattresses
Class 500	Less than 1 lb/cu ft	Gold dust, bags of air, low-density freight
How LTL Pricing Works

LTL rates are calculated using freight class, shipment weight, and lane distance. Carriers apply a rate per hundredweight (CWT) from their published tariff, then apply negotiated discounts. Additional accessorial charges (liftgate, residential delivery, appointment, fuel surcharge) are added to produce the total invoice.

Frequently Asked Questions About LTL Freight
What does LTL stand for in shipping?

LTL stands for Less Than Truckload - a freight shipping method where a shipper's cargo does not fill an entire truck, so multiple shippers share space on the same trailer.

How is LTL freight priced?

LTL pricing is based on freight class (NMFC class 50–500), shipment weight, origin and destination lane, and applicable accessorial charges. Carriers apply a rate per hundredweight (CWT) with negotiated discounts off published tariff.

What is the maximum weight for LTL shipping?

Most LTL carriers accept shipments up to 15,000 lbs. Shipments above these thresholds typically require a volume LTL (VLTL) quote or partial truckload (PTL) arrangement.

How long does LTL shipping take?

Regional lanes (1–3 states) typically transit in 1–3 business days. Cross-country lanes may take 5–7 business days or longer due to terminal sorting and consolidation.

What is Telematics? How Fleet Telematics Transforms Trucking Operations
